content: Idiopathic hypercalciuria is a hereditary metabolic condition characterized by excessive calcium excretion in the urine, despite normal serum calcium levels. This condition is associated with significant morbidity, primarily due to kidney stone formation and bone demineralization, which can lead to osteopenia and osteoporosis. Individuals with idiopathic hypercalciuria are predisposed to developing calcium oxalate and calcium phosphate kidney stones throughout their lives. In some cases, calcium crystals may accumulate in the renal interstitium, resulting in elevated calcium levels within the kidneys. In children, idiopathic hypercalciuria can manifest as recurrent macroscopic or microscopic hematuria, frequency-dysuria syndrome, urinary tract infections, and abdominal or lumbar pain. Various dietary strategies have been proposed to reduce urinary calcium levels or prevent urinary crystallization. The primary aim of this review was to evaluate the efficacy, effectiveness, and safety of dietary interventions in preventing complications such as urolithiasis and osteopenia in both adults and children with idiopathic hypercalciuria. Additionally, the review sought to assess the potential benefits of dietary interventions in alleviating urological symptoms in children with this condition. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and quasi-RCTs that investigated dietary interventions for preventing complications of idiopathic hypercalciuria. These interventions were compared to placebo, no intervention, or other dietary strategies, regardless of the method of administration, dosage, or duration. Data were extracted using standardized forms, and outcomes were analyzed using risk ratios (RR) for dichotomous data and mean differences (MD) for continuous data, both with 95% confidence intervals (CI). Five studies involving 379 adult participants were included in the review. Due to the heterogeneity of the interventions studied, data could not be pooled. The methodological quality of the studies was generally poor, with inadequate reporting of random sequence generation, allocation methods, and blinding. However, selective reporting bias was deemed low. One study involving 120 participants compared a low-calcium diet to a diet with normal calcium, low protein, and low salt over five years. The latter diet significantly reduced the recurrence of kidney stones (RR 0.77, 95% CI 0.61 to 0.98), decreased oxaluria (MD 78.00 µmol/d, 95% CI 26.48 to 129.52), and lowered the calcium oxalate relative supersaturation index (MD 1.20, 95% CI 0.21 to 2.19). Another study with 210 participants compared a low-salt, normal-calcium diet to a broader diet over three months. The low-salt, normal-calcium diet significantly reduced urinary calcium excretion (MD -45.00 mg/d, 95% CI -74.83 to -15.17) and oxalate excretion (MD -4.00 mg/d, 95% CI -6.44 to -1.56). A smaller study involving 17 participants examined the effects of dietary fiber as part of a low-calcium, low-oxalate diet over three weeks. While urinary calcium levels decreased, oxaluria increased. Another small study involving 20 participants investigated the use of Phyllanthus niruri plant substrate in individuals with hypercalciuria over three months but found no significant effect on urinary calcium levels. A crossover study with 12 participants evaluated the impact of consuming calcium-fortified orange juice or milk for one month and found no measurable benefits. None of the included studies reported significant adverse effects associated with the dietary interventions. In conclusion, long-term adherence to a diet with normal calcium levels, low protein, and low salt over five years may reduce kidney stone recurrence, oxaluria, and calcium oxalate supersaturation in individuals with idiopathic hypercalciuria who experience recurrent kidney stones. Short-term adherence to a low-salt, normal-calcium diet can also reduce urinary calcium and oxalate excretion. However, other dietary interventions examined in the included studies did not demonstrate significant benefits. No studies were identified that evaluated the effects of dietary recommendations on other clinical complications or asymptomatic idiopathic hypercalciuria.
